name: Medial approach to the proximal tibia (periprosthetic knee)
corridor: Straight or slightly curved cut from the medial epicondyle to the posteromedial tibial border, reflecting or elevating pes anserinus while leaving the MCL on bone

positioning.text: If the hip is mobile, place the patient supine with the limb abducted, externally rotated, and in a figure-of-4. If the hip is stiff, use lateral decubitus with the involved limb down. A proximal-thigh tourniquet may be used.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the medial epicondyle and the posteromedial tibial border with the knee slightly flexed.

incision.text: Make a straight or slightly curved cut from the medial epicondyle toward the posteromedial tibial edge and extend it as needed.

superficial_interval.text: Open fascia over semimembranosus and expose the pes anserinus.

deep_interval.text: Reflect the pes tendons posteriorly, or elevate their broad insertion from anterior, to see the posteromedial and medial tibia. Do not elevate the MCL from its insertion; a plate may sit over the MCL with care.

layers.text: Skin, fascia, pes anserinus, MCL on bone, then the medial and posteromedial tibia.

structures_at_risk.text: The MCL is closely adherent to bone anteriorly and proximally; lifting it destabilizes the knee.

danger_zones.text: The MCL insertion is the danger zone. Do not strip it to seat a plate.

retraction_hazards.text: Elevating pes from anterior does not create instability if the MCL is left on bone.

exposure.text: Shows the medial and posteromedial tibial edge for plating around a TKA.

limitations.text: A stiff hip forces lateral-decubitus positioning. The MCL cannot be used as a dissection plane.

indications.text: Used for medial or posteromedial proximal-tibial periprosthetic fracture fixation.

closure.text: Insert drains if needed and close the soft tissues routinely.

complications.text: The principal complication is knee instability from MCL elevation.

procedure_applications.condition: A medial or posteromedial proximal-tibial periprosthetic fracture is plated over an intact MCL

questions.question: How is the limb positioned if the hip is mobile?
questions.answer: Supine, abducted and externally rotated, in a figure-of-4.

questions.question: May the MCL be elevated from bone?
questions.answer: No. Elevation of its insertion can destabilize the knee. A plate may lie over an intact MCL.

questions.question: How can pes anserinus be handled?
questions.answer: Reflected posteriorly, or elevated from anterior without creating instability.
